ed81272792.q: What are the four color personality types defined in Surrounded by Idiots by Thomas Erickson?
ed81272792.a: The four color personality types are: Red, which are very dominant and results-driven people; Yellow, which are outgoing, very talkative and likable people; Green, with approximately 80% of the UK population being Green and described as really nice people; and Blue, which are very critical, task-oriented people who need all the answers and data.
ed81272792.e: Are We the Idiots? A Colourful Team Reflection | Pax8 - The Athena Rebels Podcast Episode 7
f: Thomas Erickson's framework divides people into four color-based personality types: Red personalities are dominant and results-driven , Yellow personalities are outgoing and talkative, Green personalities are described as genuinely nice and represent approximately 80% of the UK population, and Blue personalities are critical and task-oriented, requiring detailed data before decisions.

The color personality model emerged as a practical tool for understanding team dynamics. When the Academy team at Pax8 adopted this framework , they faced a common organizational challenge: a newly assembled group blending different nationalities, skill sets, and working styles. The color system provided an accessible language for recognizing those differences rather than dismissing them as personality clashes.
The four colors in depth

Red personalities drive toward measurable outcomes and control . They operate with urgency and decisiveness, making them natural leaders in fast-paced environments. They tend to prioritize results over process, which can make them appear impatient to other types. As discussed in this episode of The Athena Rebels Podcast , recognizing this trait helps teams avoid misinterpreting their directness as rudeness.

Yellow personalities energize through connection and communication . They are naturally sociable, persuasive, and focused on relationships. Their enthusiasm can mobilize teams and their ability to engage others makes them valuable in client-facing or collaborative roles. Yet they may sometimes prioritize interaction over detailed analysis.

Green personalities comprise roughly 80% of the UK population according to Erickson's data. They are characterized as patient, reliable, and genuinely considerate of others. Greens value stability and harmony, often acting as the backbone of organizational culture. They tend to avoid conflict and may struggle with rapid change, but their steadiness builds trust across teams.

f: Every person in your organization influences the customer journey at some point. A negative interaction anywhere—whether from finance, support, or operations—can damage how customers view your entire business. Sales is not a single pitch; it's the collective responsibility of building and maintaining relationships across every touchpoint.

When customers engage with your organization, they don't segment their experience by department. A poor interaction in billing, onboarding, or customer support registers as a reflection of your company as a whole. Sales is not a single transaction— it's a continuous process involving multiple interactions at different stages . A receptionist greeting a prospect sets the tone. Finance clarifying pricing demonstrates professionalism and reliability. Implementation teams ensure the customer actually receives value. Each interaction either strengthens or weakens the relationship.

This is why training employees beyond the sales team is critical. When someone from operations understands they're helping close or retain a deal, they approach their work with a different mindset. f: Keeping in touch days are essential for easing parents back into the workplace, allowing them to remain abreast of changes and maintain connection to colleagues and business direction. These should be part of a comprehensive re-onboarding process rather than a one-day orientation, extending throughout the entire employee journey.
Beyond the first day: structured re-onboarding over time

A single orientation day is insufficient for parents returning from maternity leave. The transition back to work involves far more than a refresh on office procedures—it requires gradual reintegration into team dynamics, updated systems, and organizational changes that have occurred during absence. As discussed in The Athena Rebels Podcast , this is where keeping in touch days prove crucial.

Keeping in touch days allow employees to visit the workplace, reconnect with colleagues, and stay informed about business priorities before their full return. This strategy reduces the shock of re-entry and helps parents mentally prepare for juggling professional responsibilities with parenting demands. The approach acknowledges that returning from maternity leave isn't a single event—it's a process.
Why this matters: the reality of returning mothers in the UK tech sector

The context behind this strategy is stark: 80 percent of UK mothers report that returning to work after maternity leave is very tough . In the tech sector specifically, the challenge is even sharper, with over 50 percent of women in UK tech leaving by age 35. These figures underscore why thoughtful onboarding isn't a nice-to-have—it's a retention and wellbeing imperative.

This manifests as reluctance to be seen leaving early or guilt-driven overwork late into evenings to compensate for perceived absences — a self-imposed barrier that undermines genuine reintegration.
The Perception Trap: When Self-Doubt Becomes the Real Obstacle

Returning to work after maternity leave is already challenging. But for many parents, the hardest part isn't external — it's internal. The anxiety about being judged by colleagues creates a feedback loop of overcompensation that keeps returning parents in a cycle of guilt and exhaustion.

This emotional barrier operates silently. A parent might feel unable to leave at a reasonable time because leaving "early" signals that they're not fully committed. Conversely, they compensate by staying late, working through breaks, or taking on extra projects they don't have capacity for. The result is burnout disguised as dedication.

As explored in The Athena Rebels Podcast , this pattern affects not just the individual but their ability to show up authentically at work. When a parent is operating from a place of fear and self-imposed pressure, genuine collaboration, creativity, and team connection become nearly impossible.

4dd564c889.q: How can individuals proactively manage their own reintegration into the workplace after extended leave?
4dd564c889.a: If an organization does not provide structured onboarding, individuals should take intentional action by scheduling meetings with their manager to…

f: Take proactive control by scheduling structured meetings with your manager to understand business changes and reset clear goals , dedicating time to reconnect with colleagues across your team, and actively investigating how organizational structures have evolved during your absence. This self-directed approach works even when formal onboarding isn't provided.
Three steps to own your return

The first move is intentional conversation with your direct manager. Rather than waiting for a formal reintegration plan, book time to discuss what's shifted —new projects, team restructures, process changes, business priorities. This meeting isn't just a catch-up; it's your chance to anchor yourself to the current reality and jointly define what success looks like in your role over the next quarter. Lamara Thorne outlines this strategy in The Athena Rebels Podcast , drawing from her own experience navigating return to work.

Reconnecting with colleagues matters just as much as the manager conversation. Dedicate specific time to one-on-one conversations with team members and adjacent departments. Ask what they've shipped, what problems they've solved, what's stressed them. This rebuilds trust, restores your informal knowledge network, and positions you as genuinely interested in others' work—not just your own job. These touchpoints also often surface informal changes that formal updates might miss.

Finally, become a detective about organizational evolution. Look at your company org chart, review recent communications, attend all-hands meetings, and ask your peers open questions about team and business structure shifts. Understanding the landscape prevents you from operating on outdated mental models and helps you locate the people and resources you'll need. This active learning is entirely in your control, regardless of whether your employer offers structured onboarding.

8a3d86c98d.q: What is the core principle of the Let Them Theory as a mindset shift?
8a3d86c98d.a: The Let Them Theory is about stopping trying to control other people's choices because you can't—you can only control your own. It's the notion of stop trying to control other people's kind of choices because you can't, you can only control your own. The theory emphasizes focusing on what you are actually responsible for rather than wasting energy on situations beyond your control.
8a3d86c98d.e: The Let Them Theory: The Mindset Shift Everyone Needs | Pax8 - The Athena Rebels Podcast Episode 11
f: The Let Them Theory teaches you to stop trying to control other people's choices because you fundamentally cannot —you can only control your own decisions and actions. By shifting your focus to what you are actually responsible for, you reclaim energy that was being wasted on situations beyond your control.

The core insight is deceptively simple: most of the stress we experience comes from attempting to manage outcomes we don't own. At work, in relationships, in leadership—we exhaust ourselves trying to shape choices that belong to someone else. The Let Them Theory invites you to release that burden.

As discussed in this episode of The Athena Rebels Podcast , the theory emphasizes that this shift is empowering, not permissive —it's not about ignoring problems or dodging responsibility. Instead, it's about drawing a clear boundary between what belongs to you and what doesn't.
The Boundary Between Your Responsibility and Theirs

The real power of this mindset lies in distinguishing what you can actually influence. You are responsible for your own effort, your communication, your integrity, and the clarity of what you ask of others. You are not responsible for whether they choose to follow through, believe what you say, or make the decisions you'd prefer.

This distinction matters most in high-stakes environments—sales teams, leadership roles, family systems. Sophie Dowsett-Smith explores how this principle applies to workplaces like Pax8, where managers often find themselves emotionally drained from trying to fix choices made by their teams.

f: When someone irritates or disagrees with you, pause for five seconds, count in your head, and tell yourself "let them" before responding. This creates space between you, the other person, and the situation, allowing you to refocus your attention back on yourself and respond consciously rather than react emotionally.

The method is straightforward and can be deployed in any moment of friction. Rather than defaulting to an immediate reaction—which often escalates tension or leads to words you regret—the five-second pause gives your brain time to shift from reactive mode to responsive mode.

Saying "let them" internally serves as a mental anchor, a short phrase that signals to yourself that you're deliberately stepping away from trying to control or fix the other person's thoughts, feelings, or choices. This reframes the situation as one where you reclaim your own agency instead of being pulled into their emotional space.

As explored in The Athena Rebels Podcast , this approach is not about passivity or avoiding difficult conversations. Instead, it's an empowering tool that helps you engage from a place of clarity and choice rather than reactivity.

The beauty of the five-second technique is that it's portable—you can use it in meetings, in one-on-one conversations, via email, or even in text exchanges. The moment you feel the irritation or disagreement rising, you have a concrete intervention available to you right then.

f: Stop the self-criticism by recognizing that what others have achieved doesn't diminish your own potential . The Let Them Theory teaches you to let others get on with their path while you focus entirely on yours—you don't know the full picture of what it took them to get there, and obsessing over their progress only stalls your own.

Envy at work often masquerades as legitimate concern about your own progress. In reality, it's a form of self-inflicted torture. When you catch yourself thinking someone else has a better salary, a higher position, or more impressive material success, you're not actually gathering useful information—you're feeding a comparison loop that erodes your energy and focus.

The core insight here is simple: you have zero control over what others choose to do or achieve . What you do have control over is where you direct your attention and effort. Every minute spent wondering why someone else got promoted is a minute you're not investing in your own development or clarity about what you actually want.

As the hosts explore in the episode , this mindset shift isn't about pretending obstacles don't exist or avoiding responsibility for your own choices. It's about reclaiming your mental and emotional energy from the comparison trap and investing it in deliberate action on your own priorities.
From self-judgment to intentional focus

Comparison torture typically starts with a small thought: "They got promoted faster than I did." But the real damage comes next, when you internalize it as "This means something about me." That's where self-criticism becomes the actual barrier —not the other person's success, but your reaction to it.

Setting Boundaries, Not Stepping Back

The core distinction lies in intentionality. Passivity means doing nothing—staying silent, tolerating issues, accepting disrespect. Let Them Theory, by contrast, is active and deliberate: you pause before reacting , assess what's within your control, and then act from a place of clarity rather than frustration.

The method has three concrete steps. First, you pause—often using a five-second count to interrupt the automatic reaction. Second, you redirect your energy into what you can actually control : your boundaries, your voice, your choices. Third, you set those boundaries without over-explaining or justifying yourself to others. This framework has resonated so widely that the concept became a number one bestseller on Amazon in 2024 and gained viral momentum on TikTok, where people even got tattoos of "let them" as a reminder.

The key insight: you own your voice while protecting your resources . You're not abandoning responsibility—you're reclaiming agency by refusing to let others' behavior dictate your emotional state or drain your time.

As explored in this episode of The Athena Rebels Podcast , the theory applies directly to workplace dynamics—especially when colleagues or leaders are making choices you disagree with or that frustrate you. Rather than absorb that frustration or try to manage them, you acknowledge the situation, set your boundary, and move forward.

Burnout doesn't happen by accident—it's the direct result of missing or unclear boundaries. Boundaries create the safety teams need

When leaders and teams embrace this approach, something shifts. Psychological safety emerges when people understand their parameters —what they're responsible for, what they're not, and where the lines truly are. This clarity removes the anxiety of overstepping or falling short, which is one of the largest drivers of workplace stress.

The mechanism is straightforward: clear boundaries mean people know what to focus on. When people understand exactly what they're working with , they can perform at their best instead of wasting energy on decisions, problems, or emotions that belong to someone else. This has a direct, measurable impact on both individual wellbeing and team output.

This principle is especially powerful in cultures where boundaries are rarely modeled or discussed. Many organizations inadvertently reward boundary-crossing—staying late, solving others' problems, absorbing stress—which eventually leads to burnout. The Let Them Theory reverses that dynamic by making boundaries an explicit, supported part of how work gets done, as detailed in the podcast discussion .
